blocks.title: Scope: counselling and recognition
blocks.text: For the pharmacist/IP, this page covers recognising types, setting expectations, safety and referral. It is **not** a procedure how-to (no injection technique, laser settings or peel recipes).

head: Procedure
What it is
rows: Controlled chemical injury to the epidermis ± dermis to resurface skin (photoageing, pigment, fine lines, acne, superficial scars)
Collagen induction therapy: fine needles (professional about 0.5–3 mm; home devices much shorter) create micro-injuries that trigger new collagen
Selective photothermolysis: the wavelength targets a chromophore (water, haemoglobin or melanin)

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Each procedure injures the skin in a controlled way, triggering inflammation, re-epithelialisation and collagen remodelling. **‘Frosting’** (whitening) with some peel agents, such as TCA, reflects protein coagulation and indicates depth. This is for recognition only.
Microneedling microchannels close within minutes and the epidermis is largely preserved, so it often suits darker skin better than ablative options.

head: Depth
Example agents
Downtime (approx.)
Common aims
rows: About a week of crusting and swelling
Texture, freckling, AKs, fine lines, some scars

head: Class
Examples
Use (overview)
rows: Deep wrinkles and scars; more downtime and risk
Microscopic columns with skin bridges left intact
Atrophic acne scars, photoageing; faster healing
Telangiectasia, redness, **pink hypertrophic scars**, some vascular birthmarks
Specialist; melasma often relapses and laser can **worsen PIH**

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: There is no disease to diagnose. Instead, the **pre-procedure assessment** covers: Fitzpatrick type, **HSV history**, **isotretinoin status**, keloid tendency, pregnancy, sun exposure, active acne or infection, and realistic goals.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Laser hair removal; fractional lasers; pigment lasers; fractional RF microneedling; superficial and medium peels; microdermabrasion; dermaroller; biopsies; superficial excisions
ddx.f: **Deep** phenol peels; fully ablative resurfacing; mechanical dermabrasion

blocks: The old rule was to delay elective procedures for **about 6 months after isotretinoin**, because of theoretical impaired healing and scarring. A task force review (Mysore et al., *Standard Guidelines of Care*), cited in Module 6, found **insufficient evidence** to support a blanket delay for many procedures.

head: Generally considered acceptable (in experienced hands)
Still a higher-risk discussion
rows: Laser hair removal; fractional lasers; pigment lasers; fractional RF microneedling; **superficial and medium peels**; microdermabrasion; dermaroller; biopsies; superficial excisions
**Deep** phenol peels; fully ablative resurfacing; mechanical dermabrasion

ul: **Do not** perform medium or deep peels or procedures without the appropriate training, governance and insurance.

**Isotretinoin:** do **not** clear patients for procedures yourself. Document isotretinoin use and **refer the decision to the operating clinician**. Some UK centres remain conservative. Continue standard isotretinoin safety (pregnancy prevention programme, blood tests, mucocutaneous effects).
**Aftercare counselling:** gentle cleansing, **SPF**, moisturiser, no picking, and expect temporary redness, peeling or swelling.
**Antiviral prophylaxis** may be advised by the operator if there is a history of HSV.
**Home microneedling rollers:** warn about infection and poor hygiene or quality.
**PIH or hypopigmentation** (especially darker skin), scarring, burns, blistering
Acne flare, persistent redness, granulomatous reactions (products driven into the skin with needling)

refer.t: Pain, spreading redness, pus or fever after a procedure: infection.
Grouped vesicles after a facial procedure: **HSV**, needing prompt antivirals.
Blistering, burns or dyspigmentation: refer back to the operator or dermatology.
Deep peels: systemic toxicity risk. Specialist settings only.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Pain, spreading redness, pus or fever after a procedure: infection.
Grouped vesicles after a facial procedure: **HSV**, needing prompt antivirals.
Blistering, burns or dyspigmentation: refer back to the operator or dermatology.
Deep peels: systemic toxicity risk. Specialist settings only.

pearls: **More ablative is not always better.** Match downtime and risk to the goal and skin type.
Darker skin: start cautiously, as there is a higher risk of dyspigmentation and keloid.
Pregnancy: most elective peels and lasers are deferred.
Advise patients to check the provider’s **qualifications and insurance**.
Patient phrase: “Many modern guidelines no longer insist on a blanket 6-month wait for milder procedures, but your dermatologist or cosmetic clinician decides case by case.”
